## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. Which `dplyr` verb keeps only the rows where `carrier == &quot;DL&quot;`?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>`select()`</li>
  <li>`filter()`</li>
  <li>`arrange()`</li>
  <li>`mutate()`</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> `filter()` keeps rows matching a logical condition. `select()` picks columns; `arrange()` sorts rows; `mutate()` creates new columns.</div>
:::


## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Recognize when a dataset is in *tidy format* (each variable a column, each observation a row)
- Convert a "wide" dataset to tidy format with `tidyr::pivot_longer()` (and back with `pivot_wider()`)
- Import spreadsheet data into R from CSV files using `readr::read_csv()`
- Identify the role of the `tidyverse` "umbrella" package

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

## Check-in: Importing data

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. A dataset is in *tidy* format when:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>It has no missing values</li>
  <li>Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each observational unit has its own table</li>
  <li>The data is sorted alphabetically</li>
  <li>The column names are in lowercase</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Tidy data is about *structure*, not contents. Wickham's three rules are: variables in columns, observations in rows, observational units in their own tables. Tidy is unrelated to whether data is &quot;clean&quot; (free of errors or missing values).</div>
:::

## Check-in: Tidy data

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. What does `pivot_longer()` do?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Sorts a data frame by the longest column</li>
  <li>Adds new columns to a data frame</li>
  <li>Reshapes data from wide format to long/tidy format</li>
  <li>Joins two data frames</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> `pivot_longer()` collapses multiple columns into key/value pairs, producing a longer (and usually tidier) data frame. The inverse is `pivot_wider()`.</div>
:::

<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. When would you use `read_csv()` instead of base R's `read.csv()`?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>When the file is very small</li>
  <li>When you want a `tibble` and faster, more predictable parsing</li>
  <li>Only when the file is online</li>
  <li>They are exactly equivalent</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> `readr::read_csv()` returns a `tibble`, doesn't auto-convert strings to factors, gives clearer messages, and is faster on large files.</div>
:::

## Check-in: `tidyverse` package

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A data frame has columns `country`, `1990`, `1995`, `2000`, `2005` — population values per country per year. Why is this **NOT** tidy?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Column names cannot start with numbers</li>
  <li>The years should be *values* of a `year` variable, not *names* of separate columns</li>
  <li>The country values are repeated</li>
  <li>It's missing a primary key</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Variables (here, `year` and `population`) belong in their own columns. Encoding `year` in *column names* means the year variable is hidden in metadata. `pivot_longer(cols = -country, names_to = &quot;year&quot;, values_to = &quot;population&quot;)` fixes it.</div>
:::
